mcqs.question: You've found one serious bug and about fifteen minor style issues in a PR. What's the best way to leave the review?
options: Lead with a summary comment naming the one blocking issue, prefix the rest `nit:`, and cut the nits a formatter should own
Post all sixteen comments so the author has the complete picture and can decide what to act on
Post only the blocking bug and silently fix the style issues yourself after merge
Request changes citing the bug, and hold the style comments for a second round after it's fixed
mcqs.explanation: Signal buried under volume is the same as no signal — the author drowning in sixteen comments applies the least-thought fix to the one that mattered. Prioritizing for the author is the reviewer's job; dumping everything shifts that work onto them, fixing things silently removes the learning, and holding comments back turns one round trip into a ping-pong review.

mcqs.question: A reviewer clicked Request changes, you addressed the comment two days ago, and they're now on vacation for a week. What should the team's process allow?
options: Merging with an admin override, since the comment was addressed
A written stale-block rule letting another code owner resolve a change request that gets no response within 24 hours of the author replying
Closing the PR and reopening it so the block is cleared
Waiting — a blocking review is a deliberate signal and only its author should clear it
mcqs.explanation: The point of writing the rule down is that using it stops being a social act — the author isn't overruling a colleague, they're following policy. Waiting a week blocks delivery on someone who isn't refusing but is simply absent, while admin overrides and reopen tricks route around review entirely and leave no record that the concern was handled.

mcqs.question: A reviewer who wasn't part of the design discussion questions the whole architecture on your implementation PR. When is reopening the decision legitimate rather than gatekeeping?
options: When the reviewer is more senior than the people who made the original decision
When the PR hasn't been approved yet, since nothing is settled until merge
When they bring information the design discussion didn't have — a new constraint, a benchmark, or an incident
Never — decisions recorded in a design doc are final until the next planning cycle
mcqs.explanation: New information is what distinguishes a real concern from a preference that wasn't voiced in time; without it, the same question that was valuable three weeks ago now costs a week and asks the author to defend a decision they didn't make alone. Seniority isn't the test, and treating decisions as permanently unchallengeable is the opposite failure — the point is redirecting to the design forum, not refusing to revisit.

mcqs.question: You believe a PR's logic belongs in the domain layer, not the controller. What's the best way to raise that?
options: Leave inline comments on each affected method showing the version you'd have written
Approve it and open your own follow-up PR restructuring it the way you'd prefer
Request changes with a link to the layering convention and let the author work out the implications
One top-level comment stating the concern, followed by a short call before the author rewrites anything
mcqs.explanation: A structural disagreement is one conversation, not eighteen inline round trips at hours apart — saying it once and moving to a call decides in fifteen minutes what a comment thread spends two days on. Reconstructing your preferred version comment by comment is design-by-comment, and silently rewriting it yourself afterwards takes the learning away from the author entirely.

mcqs.question: Your team's median time-to-merge has doubled since tightening review standards. What tells you whether that friction is healthy?
options: Whether the change failure rate fell over the same period
Whether reviewers are leaving more comments per PR than before
Whether engineers report the review process feels more rigorous
Whether the extra time is spent on design comments rather than style comments
mcqs.explanation: Friction is only healthy if it buys defect prevention, so the outcome metric — fewer defects reaching production — is the one that settles it; slower delivery with an unchanged failure rate is pure tax no matter how it feels. Comment counts and perceived rigor are trivially gamed, and even design-focused comments can be preference-driven relitigation rather than catches.

mcqs.question: A team has 100% review coverage, fast approvals and a high approval rate — yet two of the last three incidents came from bugs visible in approved diffs. What's the most effective first move?
options: Raise the required approver count from one to two on all PRs
Add a review-standards section to the engineering handbook and share it in the team channel
Set a team goal of a minimum number of substantive comments per review
Show the team the incident-to-diff trace, then change one structural constraint such as a PR size cap, and re-measure
mcqs.explanation: The dashboard looks excellent precisely because these metrics measure activity rather than value, so recovery has to start with evidence people can't argue with, followed by a constraint that changes behavior. A comment-count target is instantly gamed into comments about nothing, a second approver usually adds diffusion of responsibility rather than scrutiny, and a handbook page changes no one's incentives.
